overview: Algeria has no visible dedicated femtech startup scene, so the women's-health picture is driven by public health and policy rather than private products. Maternal mortality has fallen to around 62 per 100,000, but screening gaps remain stark: most breast cancers are still found by self-examination and Algeria has not introduced HPV vaccination. A 2023-2027 national digital health strategy and a small but growing women-in-tech accelerator pipeline are the most plausible foundations for future femtech, though neither yet targets women's health specifically.

sections.heading: Recent developments
sections.narrative: Coverage centres on cancer epidemiology and menstrual-health awareness rather than product launches, reflecting a public-health rather than commercial femtech landscape.

items.text: Algeria adopted its Stratégie Nationale de Santé Numérique (National Digital Health Strategy) 2023-2027, covering electronic health records and telemedicine to reach remote areas.
UNFPA reported that in an Arab-region survey including Algeria, 40% of women and girls had no information about menstruation before their first period, with many reporting shame and fear.
A multicentre real-world study of 6,044 Algerian breast-cancer patients across 23 oncology centres found 67.7% of tumours were detected by self-examination and only 4.2% via screening.
Trends in Maternal Mortality 2000-2023 (WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank, UNDESA) placed Algeria's maternal mortality ratio at roughly 62 per 100,000 live births.

sections.heading: Policy and public health
sections.narrative: Women's-health policy in Algeria runs through the health ministry, UNFPA cooperation and national cancer control, with digital health still at an early framework stage.

items.text: The 2023-2027 National Digital Health Strategy prioritises electronic health records and telemedicine, but the primary text is not published on the health ministry portal and implementation detail is thin.
UNFPA works with the Algerian government on voluntary family planning, safe motherhood and comprehensive sexuality education delivered through community, parental and religious-leader outreach.

HPV vaccination is still not part of Algeria's national programme, unlike neighbouring Tunisia which is introducing a school-based HPV vaccine, leaving cervical-cancer prevention reliant on screening.
Contraceptive prevalence is most recently reported at 57.1% (2012/13); across two-thirds of Arab states prevalence sits below 60%, indicating unmet need for modern family planning.

sections.heading: Women's-health and women-in-tech ecosystem
sections.narrative: There is no identifiable Algeria-based femtech company; the nearest relevant infrastructure is a general startup and women-in-tech accelerator ecosystem plus UN and research actors working on women's health.

items.name: Algeria startup accelerator ecosystem
items.note: A domestic accelerator and incubator scene exists but is general-purpose; no women's-health vertical has emerged from it to date.

sections.heading: Research and evidence
sections.narrative: Peer-reviewed studies and UN reports are the strongest evidence base for Algerian women's health, particularly on cancer, maternal mortality and menstrual awareness.
